Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A gray tabby cat curled asleep on a yellow knit blanket on a wooden windowsill, a blue wall behind and leaves through the window

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

21 stepsCanvas: 16 x 12 inFocal point: The cat's sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose, the whiskers and the white paws tucked under the chin Light: Daylight from the window at the upper left, lighting the left of the cat's head, the top of the blanket and a patch of the sillHow this lesson was made

Tubes to get out

Get these out of the box before you start. Every paint in the lesson is mixed from them; squeeze out a little of each when its step comes up.

  • Titanium whitefirst in step 1
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)first in step 1
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)first in step 1
  • Ultramarine bluefirst in step 1
  • Burnt siennafirst in step 3

What you need

Brushes

  • 3/4 inch wash brush: Blend the sky in the windowFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff brush: Dab the dark leavesOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • 1 inch wide flat: Blend the blue wallFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/2 inch flat: Block in the window frameFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1/4 inch flat: Shade the frame's inner sidesFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 1 inch flat: Block in the windowsillFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • 3/4 inch flat: Shade the sill's front edgeFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #8 round: Tap in the dark knit loopsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #6 round: Tap in the light knit loopsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/4 inch angle: Pull the dark tabby stripesAngle: flat cut on a slant, for crisp corners and curves
  • #4 round: Paint the pink inside the earsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • small fan brush: Flick in the light furFan: bristles spread like a fan, for grass, fur, and soft blending
  • #1 liner: Line the closed eyes and mouthLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 16 x 12 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Using another size? Scale every measurement.
  • A ruler
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Before you start

Placing shapes with a transfer outline optional

The transfer outline (optional)

The outlines of the main shapes, on a grid of quarters: 1 The white window frame; 2 The wooden windowsill; 3 The yellow knit blanket; 4 The sleeping tabby cat. On your 16 x 12 in canvas the grid lines are 4 in apart across and 3 in apart down. Before the stage that starts one, you can lightly chalk its outline on the canvas, measuring from the edges with a ruler.

Strokes to try on scrap paper first

Each one's card is open in the step that first uses it.

  • Side-to-side blend, first in step 1.
  • Dabbing, first in step 2.
  • Building from pieces, first in step 5.
  • Dry brush, first in step 8. Try it on scrap paper first: wipe the brush until it leaves broken marks.
  • Press and lift, first in step 11. Try a row of them on scrap paper first.
  • Curved strokes, first in step 14.
  • Thick to thin, first in step 16.
  • Flicking, first in step 18.
  • Liner work, first in step 20. Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

Getting started

The other basics are in the steps where they matter.

Before you start

Not checked yet

  • Two water jars: one to rinse the brush, one kept clean for thinning paint. A big clear jar shows when the rinse water is dirty.
  • A rag or paper towel, to wipe the brush between colors.
  • Put out bigger puddles of paint than you think you need. Big puddles stay wet longer than small smears.
  • Lay your colors out the same way every time, so they're easy to find and don't get dragged into each other.

Keep your colors clean

Not checked yet

  • Wipe the brush on a rag between colors.
  • Rinse it fully before going into white.
  • Rinse often. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  • Mix on the palette, not on the canvas. Two or three colors at most: stop when the color is right.

Keep paint from drying on the palette

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic on a brushstroke stays wet for only a few minutes.
  • Mist the palette lightly with a spray bottle now and then. Only lightly: too much water weakens the paint.
  • Cover the paint when you aren't using it.

Paint thickness and how much is on the brush

Not checked yet

  • Each step's Load line says two different things. How thick the paint is, and how much of it is on the brush. Creamy paint can be a full load or a light one.

How thick the paint is

How much is on the brush

How much water

Not checked yet

  • Keep water to about half the mix or less. More than that makes weak, see-through color that can lift when you paint over it.
  • For covering, use the paint thick, with little or no water.
  • After rinsing, wipe the metal part of the brush dry.
If something goes wrong not checked yet

Fixing a mistake

Not checked yet

  • Acrylic is forgiving. Let the area dry, then paint over it and try again.
  • Don't keep working a spot that's half dry. Leave it, work somewhere else, and come back.

The view through the window 3 steps

STEP 1 OF 21 · The view through the window, 1 of 3

Blend the sky in the window

  1. Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 1 1/4 in wide and 1 3/4 in tall.
  2. Paints, top to bottom: Pale sky blue, then Warm white.
  3. Mix enough Warm white for this step and steps 5, 15 and 21; cover it between them.
  4. Brush: 3/4 inch wash brush. Load: Creamy paint. An even coat.
  5. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.
  6. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  7. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  8. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: The light comes through this window from the upper left, so the sky is the brightest, coolest color here: keep it pale. The sky through the window reaches the left and top edges of the canvas; leave its ragged lower edge loose, as the after picture shows, because the leaves and the white window frame cover it later.

Basics: Making a color lighter or darker

Making a color lighter or darker

Not checked yet

  • To lighten: add the color to the white a little at a time, not white to the color.
  • White also dulls a color. Too much turns it chalky.
  • To darken: add the dark into the lighter mix in small amounts.
  • For the next lighter value of something, start from the mix you already have and add white, so the colors stay related.

Stroke: Side-to-side blend how to do it, not checked yet

Side-to-side blend

Not checked yet

With. wide flat; 3/4 inch wash brush

Load. Creamy paint. An even coat.

Motion. Start with the darkest color and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up the next lighter color and paint below it. Then stroke back up over the join several times.

What it leaves. Smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.

Then. Stroke back over each join while it's wet.

Blend two colors side to side

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • A hard line where two colors meet. Add more of the lighter color at the join and blend again.
  • Two very different colors won't blend. Mix a bridge color from the two on the palette (pink and yellow make orange) and paint it between them.
  • The brush is overloaded. Wipe it on a rag. Rinse before going into white.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 2 OF 21 · The view through the window, 2 of 3

Dab the dark leaves

  1. Let the sky through the window dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 1 in from the left edge; it's about 1/4 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall.
  3. The outline also runs under where the white window frame and the frame's shadows will go: paint straight through there.
  4. The outline also reaches onto the sky through the window, painted already: there, only soften this paint into its edge and leave it showing.
  5. Paint: Leaf green.
  6. Brush: old stiff brush. Load: A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.
  7. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  8. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  9. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.

Tip: Tap the clumps in loose groups and leave small gaps of the pale sky through the window between them, as the after picture shows. Make the darkest, most solid tapping along the lower part of the clumps, away from the light at the upper left. The after picture shows these marks as a deeper blue-green over the sky rather than a clear green; match its darker patches and where it leaves the pale sky.

Basics: Let each layer dry

Let each layer dry

Not checked yet

  • Between steps, the paint underneath should be dry to the touch. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  • Painting into half-dry paint drags it up and turns it gooey and muddy.
  • Thick paint can feel dry on top and still be wet inside. Give thick areas longer.
  • Fine lines and light colors over dark especially need a dry layer underneath.

STEP 3 OF 21 · The view through the window, 3 of 3

Dab the sunlit leaves

  1. Let the leaves outside the window and the sky through the window dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 1 in from the left edge; it's about 1/4 in wide and 1 1/4 in tall.
  3. The outline also runs under where the white window frame and the frame's shadows will go: paint straight through there.
  4. The outline also reaches onto the sky through the window, painted already: there, only soften this paint into its edge and leave it showing.
  5. Paint: Sunny leaf green.
  6. Brush: old stiff brush. Load: A light load. No water on the brush: a wet one makes blobs.
  7. Tap with the tip of the brush. The more you tap one spot, the more solid it gets.
  8. It should leave dots or dappled patches that get more solid the more you tap.
  9. Leave what step 2 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  10. Watch out: Blobs instead of dots. The brush is too wet or holds too much paint. Fix: wipe most of the paint off on a paper towel and tap again.
  11. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The light comes from the upper left, so tap the sunlit leaves only on the tops and left sides of the Leaf green clumps. Keep them few and small: the after picture barely changes from the step before, so leave most of the Leaf green clumps showing.

The wall and the window frame 3 steps

STEP 4 OF 21 · The wall and the window frame, 1 of 3

Blend the blue wall

  1. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  2. Inside the outlined area, all the way across from the top edge. Its bottom is about 6 in from the bottom edge.
  3. The outline also runs under where the yellow knit blanket and the wooden windowsill will go: paint straight through there.
  4. Paints, top to bottom: Wall blue, then Deep wall blue.
  5. Brush: 1 inch wide flat. Load: Creamy paint. An even coat.
  6. Start at the bottom with Deep wall blue and stroke side to side. Without rinsing, pick up Wall blue and paint above the Deep wall blue. Then stroke back and forth over the join several times.
  7. It should leave smooth bands of color, with a soft join where two wet colors meet.
  8. Watch out: Blending after the paint has started to drag. Acrylic sets in minutes, and scrubbing setting paint lifts it and leaves streaks. Fix: stop as soon as it drags.
  9. Let it dry, then blend a new thin layer on top.

Tip: Run every stroke side to side, across the whole canvas, and keep them loose: the after picture keeps soft brush marks in the blue. Paint right up to the sky through the window and the leaves outside the window, and leave them showing. The blue also goes over where the white window frame will stand, as the after picture shows.

STEP 5 OF 21 · The wall and the window frame, 2 of 3

Block in the window frame

  1. Let the blue wall dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  4. Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 4 in wide and 8 in tall.
  5. The outline also runs under where the yellow knit blanket and the wooden windowsill will go: paint straight through there.
  6. The outline also reaches onto the blue wall, painted already: there, only soften this paint into its edge and leave it showing.
  7. Paint: Warm white.
  8. Brush: 1/2 inch flat.
  9. Start with the tall upright post as one straight band, pulled from the top edge down. Then add the crossbar and the ledge as straight bars running into the post.
  10. It should leave a flat cream frame of straight bars with clean edges, with no shading yet.
  11. Warm white is much lighter than what it goes over: expect two or three thin coats, letting each dry.

Tip: Paint the tall upright post first, then the crossbar and the slanted ledge running into the post, as the after picture shows. Pull each bar along its length, and take the post on down to the bottom edge. Leave the sky through the window and the leaves outside the window showing between the bars.

Building from pieces

Not checked yet

Motion. Start with one simple shape (an oval, a circle, or a rectangle). Then add the rest in curved pieces on each side, like ( ), smaller toward the edges.

What it leaves. A shape made of distinct curved segments with small gaps or overlaps between them.

Then. Soften where the pieces meet only if the shape should look smooth; otherwise leave the pieces showing.

STEP 6 OF 21 · The wall and the window frame, 3 of 3

Shade the frame's inner sides

  1. Let the white window frame and the blue wall dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is at the top edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 4 1/2 in wide and 8 in tall.
  3. The outline also runs under where the yellow knit blanket and the wooden windowsill will go: paint straight through there.
  4. The outline also reaches onto the blue wall, painted already: there, only soften this paint into its edge and leave it showing.
  5. Paint: Lavender gray.
  6. Brush: 1/4 inch flat.
  7. Paint each shadow as a long straight band with the flat edge of the brush, pulling it the length of the bar in one stroke.
  8. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: The light comes from the window at the upper left, so keep a clean cream strip lit down the middle of the post and along the top of each bar; the shadows go on the sides and undersides, as the after picture shows. Pull each band the length of its bar, straight down the post and along the crossbar and ledge.

The windowsill 3 steps

STEP 7 OF 21 · The windowsill, 1 of 3

Block in the windowsill

  1. Let the wall and the window frame dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Optional: lightly chalk its outline first, from the transfer outline in Before you start, measuring from the canvas edges with a ruler.
  3. Inside the outlined area, all the way across to the bottom edge. Its top is about 4 1/2 in from the bottom edge.
  4. The outline also runs under where the yellow knit blanket and the sleeping tabby cat will go: paint straight through there.
  5. The outline also reaches onto the frame's shadows and the white window frame, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
  6. Paint: Warm wood brown.
  7. Mix enough Warm wood brown for this step and step 8; cover it between them.
  8. Brush: 1 inch flat.
  9. Lay one long band along the sill's top edge first, then fill in the rest of the sill in long side-to-side pieces that follow its slope.
  10. It should leave one flat, solid Warm wood brown band with no white canvas showing between the pieces.

Tip: The sill is about 16 in wide, reaching the left edge and the right edge of the canvas; its top edge runs from the foot of the white window frame and slopes down toward the right edge of the canvas, as the after picture shows. Run every stroke side to side along that slope. The after picture also shows a slightly darker band along the bottom edge of the canvas, the sill's front edge, and a thin dark lip under the white window frame; step 8 builds on both.

STEP 8 OF 21 · The windowsill, 2 of 3

Shade the sill's front edge

  1. Let the wooden windowsill, and the wall and the window frame dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 1 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is at the left edge; it's about 1 1/2 in wide and 2 in tall.
  3. The outline also runs under where the yellow knit blanket and the blanket's knit loops will go: paint straight through there.
  4. The outline also reaches onto the wooden windowsill and the frame's shadows, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
  5. Paint: Warm wood brown.
  6. Brush: 3/4 inch flat. Load: Wiped nearly dry. Only the tip goes in the paint, and no water on the brush. It should feel dry and hard to apply.
  7. Light pressure, skimming the surface.
  8. It should leave feathery, broken, see-through marks that catch the canvas texture. Never a solid area.
  9. Watch out: It went on solid. The brush was too loaded. Fix: let it dry, then dry-brush the base color back over part of it.

Tip: The light comes in through the window, so the shade goes mostly on the right side of the sill and along its front edge at the bottom edge of the canvas; leave the sunlit shapes near the white window frame as the plain base color, where the after picture has them, since step 9 lights them. Skim the strokes side to side along the sill's slope. The after picture also shows thin pale streaks marking the frame's shadow crossing the sunlit area and a few orange streaks near the front edge: copy them lightly as the after picture shows.

STEP 11 OF 21 · The blanket, 2 of 3

Tap in the dark knit loops

  1. Let the yellow knit blanket and the windowsill dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 1 in from the bottom edge, and its right side is at the right edge; it's about 14 in wide and 5 in tall.

  5. Paint: Dark ochre.
  6. Brush: #8 round. Load: Creamy paint, a full load.
  7. Touch down with the tip, press so the belly spreads, then pull and lift so the stroke ends on the tip.
  8. It should leave a teardrop or comma shape, wide where you pressed and pointed where you lifted.
  9. Watch out: A blob instead of a teardrop. Too much paint, or too slow a lift. Fix: use less paint and lift faster.

Tip: The blanket is a raised, rolled edge around a sunken middle with a fold across its front: tap the dark loops thickest where the after picture has them, in the sunken middle, under the rolled top and along the fold line. On the front, set the strokes in rows of V shapes like knit stitches; on the raised edge, run them up and down across it. Leave the yellow knit blanket showing on the tops of the rolls, where the light from the upper left falls.

The stripes and ears 2 steps

STEP 16 OF 21 · The stripes and ears, 1 of 2

Pull the dark tabby stripes

  1. Let the cat's shape and the blanket dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge, and its right side is about 1 in from the right edge; it's about 13 1/2 in wide and 6 1/2 in tall.
  4. The outline also runs under where the cat's sleeping face and the cat's fur will go: paint straight through there.
  5. The outline also reaches onto the sleeping tabby cat and the blue wall, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
  6. Paint: Charcoal.
  7. Mix enough Charcoal for this step and step 20; cover it between them.
  8. Brush: 1/4 inch angle.
  9. Press the full width of the brush for the thick part, then turn onto its edge or tip and lighten the pressure. With an angle brush, the lighter you press, the thinner the line.
  10. It should leave a line that starts wide and tapers to a point, curving around the cat's body as in the after picture.

Tip: Start each stripe wide along the top of the cat's back and pull it down around the body so it tapers to a point, following the curl of the cat; on the tail, pull short bands across it. On the head, the stripes run down from between the ears, and the after picture also darkens the ear rims and lays curved strokes where the closed eyes sit. Most of what this step adds is on the right side of the canvas, on the cat's back and tail; leave the white patches and paws clear.

  2. Inside the outlined area. Its top is about 1 1/2 in from the top edge, and its left side is about 1 in from the left edge; it's about 6 in wide and 5 1/2 in tall.
  3. The outline also reaches onto the sleeping tabby cat, and the cat's stripes and pink ears, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
  4. Paint: Charcoal.
  5. Brush: #1 liner. Load: Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.
  6. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Pull each eye as one smooth curve, starting thick and lightening toward its outer end so it tapers.
  7. It should leave thin, curved lines.
  8. Leave what step 19 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  9. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.

Tip: Each closed eye is one smooth curve that bows downward, like a smile turned over: the eye nearer the window is the longer, flatter curve, and the other sits higher and slants, as the after picture shows. Paint the eyes first, then the tiny mouth line just under the nose. The after picture also shows a few faint white whisker lines beside the face already; leave them for step 21.

  • Charcoal from step 16, mix more if it has dried2 parts ultramarine, 2 parts burnt sienna, 1 part white, a touch of yellow

With. liner; small round (the tip)

Load. Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.

Motion. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. For a tapering line, start thick and lighten as you go. Let lines fork in different directions and overlap, and wobble the edges a little.

What it leaves. Thin, flowing lines.

Then. Reload often.

Good for. branches and twigs, thick at the trunk and tapering, fine lines and details

Thin paint, upright brush

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

If it goes wrong.

  • Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Add water.
  • Lines spread or feather. The paint underneath is still wet. Only paint lines over dry paint.

Try a few lines on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 21 OF 21 · The sleeping face, 3 of 3

Pull the whiskers

  1. Let the fur, and the stripes and ears dry to the touch first. A hair dryer on low speeds it up.
  2. Rinse the brush well first. Dirty water tints every color with the last one.
  3. Inside the outlined area. Its bottom is about 5 1/2 in from the bottom edge, and its left side is about 5 1/2 in from the left edge; it's about 1/2 in wide and 1/4 in tall.
  4. The outline also reaches onto the cat's shading and white patches, and the sleeping tabby cat, painted already: there, only soften this paint into their edge and leave them showing.
  5. Paint: Warm white.
  6. Brush: #1 liner. Load: Thin paint. Swirl the brush in water, then in the paint. Add water if the line skips. Reload often.
  7. Hold the brush upright, with light, steady pressure. Start each whisker at the muzzle and pull outward, starting thick and lightening so it tapers to a fine point. Let them fan apart and cross a little.
  8. It should leave thin, tapering lines.
  9. Leave what steps 19 and 20 painted showing around these marks, as in the Result picture.
  10. Watch out: Skippy, broken lines. The paint is too thick. Fix: add water.
  11. Step back, squint, or take a photo to see it whole, and compare the big shapes with the picture.

Tip: Start each whisker at the muzzle and pull outward in a gentle curve, three or four on each side of the muzzle, fanning apart as they go, as the after picture shows. The longer ones sweep out across the gray cheek toward the white chest patch; the shorter ones sweep out over the top of the white paws. Keep them thin enough that the gray fur shows between them.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: a gray tabby kitten curled asleep on a yellow chunky-knit blanket on a wooden windowsill, a window with green leaves on the left

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: It is already a painted picture with nothing around it.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 16 x 12 in, landscape

Done: extend

Left out: nothing

Why: No canvas was named; the photo is 3:2 and the closest standard size, 16x12, is 4:3, and a crop would cut the cat's ears or the blanket, so the edges were painted on. The first extend repainted the wall as a cloudy sky; the one redo kept the plain gray-blue wall.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: No tiny separate things, no texture of hundreds of items (busy: 0.0% fine texture), no detail inside big shapes one mark can't make (the knit is one repeated chunky mark, the stripes a handful of bands), and about five parts.

Why: The picture is already a simple painting a beginner can follow.

Fine texture measured: the photo 0.0% of the canvas

A gray tabby kitten sleeps curled on a chunky yellow knit blanket on a sunny wooden sill, a window and green leaves at the upper left lighting it. The lesson is about the cat: a flat gray shape, then shading, white patches, stripes, soft fur and a quiet sleeping face, on a blanket whose knit is one repeated loop mark.

Subject: A gray tabby cat curled asleep on a yellow knit blanket on a wooden windowsill, a blue wall behind and leaves through the window
Focal point: The cat's sleeping face: the closed eyes, the pink nose, the whiskers and the white paws tucked under the chin
Light: Daylight from the window at the upper left, lighting the left of the cat's head, the top of the blanket and a patch of the sill

What it saw, back to front

  1. The sky through the window
  2. The blue wall
  3. The white window frame
  4. The wooden windowsill
  5. The yellow knit blanket
  6. The sleeping tabby cat
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front
ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A beginner paint-along on a white canvas, back to front: the wall and window, the sill, the blanket, then the cat on top. It is the only approach with version 2 keys.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

It has no version 2 keys, and the owner follows paint-along tutorials (docs/decisions.md, 2026-10-19).

How the paint recipes were worked out17 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

What the reviewer caught7 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Text check: paint Step 2: Leaf green was fitted to a pale blue-green (#83b5a2), and the step's leaves look blue rather than green. (left: renaming a paint changes the chain's requests, so it needs a new plan and chain.)
  • Text check: step Step 3: The sunlit leaf tops change almost nothing a painter would see (under 0.2% of the canvas). (left: fixing it needs a new plan and a new chain.)
  • Text check: paint Step 3: Sunny leaf green has almost nothing in the finish near its color where the plan lays it, so it keeps the plan's rough color. (left: changing it needs a new plan and chain.)
  • Text check: chain Step 4: Taking the wall off also took most of the leaves outside the window, so the first steps show a tiny window patch with almost no green, and the leaves come back on the wall step. (left: the chain checker still marks this unit after its two more tries (erase's limit).)
  • Text check: paint Step 8: The sill's shading lays the same Warm wood brown as its first coat, because its darker paint was fitted to the same color and merged into it; the picture's grain streaks come from the render, not from the paint the step names. (left: check asked for the merge; taking the step out changes the chain's units.)
  • Text check: paint Step 12: Pale yellow was fitted to a strong golden orange-yellow (#fab30f), not a pale yellow. (left: renaming a paint changes the chain's requests, so it needs a new plan and chain.)
  • Text check: paint Step 18: Light gray was fitted to a mid warm gray (#766d6f), darker than its name. (left: renaming a paint changes the chain's requests, so it needs a new plan and chain.)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • Run on pipeline v3 (--v3), from this session: the tools run here, the helpers each an Opus subagent in a fresh context.
  • Plan writer (1 subagent): given plan-brief.md, the lesson folder, 00_canvas_fit.png (no beginner version) and the technique file. Wrote 21 steps in 8 stages, 14 units, 13 renders, 10 mixes. Asked once more, with check's problem only, to merge Dark red-brown into Warm wood brown (fitted to the same color); it did, and noted shade-sill now lays its block-in's own paint. Its options were to drop the step or give the paint a darker color; I kept the plan as it was, since either change would re-render part of the chain.
  • Chain checker (1 subagent, then a fresh one after erase rewrote the looks): round 1 marked unit 2 (the wall's removal took the leaves) stray; after the redo it passed, but the fresh checker then marked unit 10 left (the white patches stayed); after that redo unit 10 passed and unit 2's stray was back, with no tries left. It stays as a known problem.
  • Stage writers: 8, whose words were thrown away when the unit 10 redo changed the pictures, then 8 more. 131 claims, 16 failed, 6 stages fixed once (also told to name only their own step's paints); final 114 claims, 2 sentences taken out (both in shade-frame, its tip kept).
  • erase asked again by itself once, for the wall left standing. Chain: 26 renders paid in all (3 runs), 49 cents.
  • Running check right after draft-text, before packets, caught the paint merge before any words were written; the cow's run lost a whole round of writers to it.
  • The canvas extend's first render repainted the wall as a cloudy sky; asking for the plain wall to stay fixed it.
